body:
Foundations of Islam

Islam originated in the Arabian Peninsula in the 7th century CE through the teachings of Prophet Muhammad. Its fundamental religious principle is Tawhid, belief in the unity and uniqueness of God.

The Quran is the central sacred scripture of Islam. Hadith refers to transmitted accounts of the sayings and actions of Prophet Muhammad. The Quran and the Prophetic tradition are important foundations of Islamic religious and ethical life.

The 5 commonly recognised pillars of Islam are the declaration of faith, prescribed prayer, charitable giving or Zakat, fasting during Ramadan and pilgrimage to Mecca for those able to undertake it.

Islam reached different parts of India through maritime trade, migration, political expansion and religious networks. Gujarat's maritime connections with western Asia were especially important in the development of its Muslim communities.

Meaning of Sufism

Sufism, also called Tasawwuf, represents the mystical and spiritual traditions within Islam. Sufi teachers emphasised inner purification, remembrance of God, love, compassion and spiritual discipline.

Sufis developed diverse approaches to religious life. Many stressed the inadequacy of outward religious observance without inner sincerity. However, Sufism should not be understood as universally rejecting Islamic law or religious practice.

Important Sufi terms

TermMeaning
Pir or MurshidSpiritual guide or teacher
MuridDisciple of a spiritual guide
SilsilaSpiritual lineage or order
KhanqahEstablishment for Sufi residence, instruction and gatherings
DargahShrine associated with the tomb of a revered saint
ZikrRemembrance of God
SamaSpiritual audition involving devotional recitation or music in certain traditions
UrsCommemoration of the death anniversary of a Sufi saint

Many Khanqahs provided spiritual instruction, hospitality and assistance to visitors. Dargahs became important pilgrimage centres, sometimes attracting visitors from diverse religious backgrounds.

Major Sufi orders in India

The Chishti order

The Chishti Silsila became one of the most influential Sufi orders in India. Many Chishti saints emphasised compassion, simplicity, spiritual instruction and hospitality towards visitors. Several prominent Chishti teachers maintained a degree of distance from political authority.

SaintPrincipal centre
Khwaja Moinuddin ChishtiAjmer, Rajasthan
Qutbuddin Bakhtiar KakiDelhi
Baba FaridPakpattan, present-day Pakistan
Nizamuddin AuliyaDelhi
Gesu DarazGulbarga, Karnataka

Amir Khusrau, an important poet and musician, was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya. His literary contributions included works in Persian and compositions associated with Hindavi traditions. He occupies a prominent place in the cultural history of Indo-Islamic devotional music.

Other important Sufi orders

  • Suhrawardi: Associated in medieval India with Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan. Some Suhrawardi teachers accepted closer relations with rulers and political institutions.
  • Qadiri: Associated with the spiritual lineage of Abdul Qadir Jilani. Mian Mir was a prominent Qadiri saint in the Indian subcontinent.
  • Naqshbandi: Associated in India with Khwaja Baqi Billah and Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi. It became known for emphasis on observance of Islamic religious principles.

The Rishi order in Kashmir, associated with Sheikh Nuruddin Wali or Nund Rishi, represents another important regional Sufi tradition.

Bhakti and Sufi cultural interaction

Many Bhakti and Sufi teachers shared an emphasis on sincere devotion, ethical conduct, love and the spiritual limitations of outward ritualism. Their teachings circulated through poetry, music, religious gatherings and oral transmission.

Nevertheless, they belonged to different religious and philosophical traditions. Sufism developed within Islamic spirituality, while Bhakti included diverse devotional traditions rooted primarily in Indian religious thought.

Sufi heritage in Gujarat

Sarkhej Roza

Sarkhej Roza, near Ahmedabad, is associated with the Sufi saint Sheikh Ahmed Khattu Ganj Bakhsh. His tomb became part of a substantial religious and architectural complex developed under the Gujarat Sultanate.

The complex contains religious buildings, royal structures and a water tank, reflecting the interaction of Sufi institutions, royal patronage and architectural development.

Shah Alam Roza

Shah Alam Roza in Ahmedabad is associated with the revered Sufi saint Shah Alam. It illustrates the continuing importance of Sufi shrines in Gujarat's religious and urban cultural history.

These sites are important not merely as monuments but as evidence of the relationship between religious teachers, communities, political patronage and Gujarat's architectural heritage.

Prelims focus

  • Tawhid refers to the unity of God in Islam.
  • A Silsila is a spiritual lineage; a Khanqah is a Sufi establishment.
  • Moinuddin Chishti is associated with Ajmer.
  • Amir Khusrau was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.
  • Sarkhej Roza is associated with Sheikh Ahmed Khattu Ganj Bakhsh.
  • Trap: A Khanqah is not necessarily a tomb shrine; a Dargah is associated with the tomb of a saint.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 110–113; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, sections on Islamic and Sufi traditions; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 7, Social Science, Chapter 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints; Gujarat Tourism, Sarkhej Roza; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Shah Alam Roza; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The Khanqah as a centre of spiritual and community life.

pictures.alt: Bhakti and Sufism remain distinct traditions while sharing sincere devotion, love, ethical conduct, poetry and religious gatherings.

title: Islam, Sufism and Indo-Islamic Cultural Traditions

body:
The religious and literary heritage of Gujarat

Gujarat developed a rich devotional culture through the interaction of Vaishnava, Shaiva, Shakta, Jain, Sant and Sufi traditions. Religious teachings circulated through poetry, storytelling, music, pilgrimage, temple worship and community service.

Gujarati saint-poets were particularly important because they expressed spiritual and ethical ideas in accessible regional language. Their compositions contributed to the development of Gujarati literature as well as living devotional practices.

Narsinh Mehta

Narsinh Mehta, also known as Narsi Mehta, was an influential 15th-century Gujarati Vaishnava saint-poet. He is traditionally associated with Talaja in Bhavnagar district and with Junagadh, where he spent a significant part of his life.

His poetry expresses devotion to Krishna, divine love, compassion and opposition to social exclusion. His religious outlook connects devotion with sensitivity towards the suffering of others.

His celebrated composition Vaishnav Jan To presents the ideal of a genuine devotee as a person who understands the suffering of others and acts without pride.

Narsinh Mehta is associated with Gujarati Pads and Prabhatiyas. Prabhatiyas are devotional compositions traditionally sung in the morning.

His devotional songs later became closely associated with Mahatma Gandhi's prayer gatherings and helped express the ethical relationship between religion and social service.

Akho or Akha Bhagat

Akho was a 17th-century Gujarati poet and philosophical thinker associated with Ahmedabad. His writings emphasise spiritual knowledge, self-realisation and the inadequacy of superficial religious practices.

His Chhappas, traditionally six-line compositions, frequently employ satire to criticise ignorance, false gurus, social hypocrisy and mechanical ritualism.

The Akhe Gita is another important work associated with his philosophical outlook. His teaching reflects the influence of Vedantic knowledge and non-dualistic thought.

While Narsinh Mehta is especially associated with Krishna devotion, Akho is particularly remembered for philosophical inquiry and criticism of religious pretence.

Vallabhacharya and Pushtimarg

Vallabhacharya, a philosopher of the late 15th and early 16th centuries, established the Vaishnava devotional tradition called Pushtimarg. Its name refers to the path of divine grace or spiritual nourishment.

Its philosophical foundation is Shuddhadvaita. Krishna is regarded as the Supreme Being, and loving devotion is understood as developing through divine grace.

Pushtimarg gives central importance to Seva, the loving service of Krishna through offerings, devotional music and worship. It recognises household life as an environment in which spiritual devotion can be practised.

The worship of Shrinathji became a central feature of this tradition. Although the major Shrinathji temple at Nathdwara is located in Rajasthan, Pushtimarg has a particularly strong historical presence in Gujarat.

Pushtimarg also encouraged devotional painting, temple music and textile traditions, including painted cloth hangings known as Pichhwais.

Dayaram

Dayaram was an important Gujarati devotional poet of the late 18th and early 19th centuries. He was associated with the Pushtimarg tradition and is particularly remembered for Krishna-centred devotional poetry.

His Garbis express devotional love, often through the relationship between Krishna and his devotees. Dayaram helped establish the Garbi as an important form of Gujarati devotional literature.

His compositions illustrate the relationship between religious philosophy, regional poetry and musical performance.

The Swaminarayan tradition

Sahajanand Swami, widely known as Swaminarayan, established an influential Hindu religious tradition in Gujarat during the early 19th century, emerging from the religious lineage of Ramanand Swami.

The tradition emphasises devotion, moral discipline, self-restraint, religious education and organised community life.

  • Shikshapatri: A Sanskrit text composed by Swaminarayan in 1826, containing 212 verses that prescribe ethical and religious conduct.
  • Vachanamrut: A collection of his religious and philosophical discourses, recorded by disciples.

Temples at Ahmedabad, Vadtal and Gadhada became important centres of the Swaminarayan tradition. Its religious institutions contributed to devotional literature, temple architecture, education and organised social service.

Jalaram Bapa

Jalaram Bapa was a 19th-century Gujarati saint associated with Virpur in Rajkot district. A devotee of Rama, he became particularly revered for charitable conduct, hospitality and service to people in need.

The tradition of providing food to visitors and those in need, commonly described as Sadavrat, is closely associated with his religious legacy.

Synthesis of major Gujarat devotional contributions

FigurePrincipal associationDistinctive contribution
Narsinh MehtaKrishna BhaktiCompassion, Pads and Prabhatiyas
AkhoVedantic knowledgeChhappas and criticism of hypocrisy
VallabhacharyaShuddhadvaitaPushtimarg and Seva
DayaramPushtimargKrishna-centred Garbis
SwaminarayanDevotional religious communityShikshapatri and moral discipline
Jalaram BapaRama BhaktiHospitality and charitable service

Prelims focus

  • Narsinh Mehta is associated with Vaishnav Jan To and Prabhatiyas.
  • Akho is particularly associated with Chhappas and Akhe Gita.
  • Vallabhacharya established Pushtimarg and taught Shuddhadvaita.
  • Dayaram is renowned for Gujarati Garbis.
  • Swaminarayan composed the Shikshapatri in 1826.
  • Jalaram Bapa is associated with Virpur in Rajkot district.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 7, Social Science, 2021–22, Chapter 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints, and Class 10, Social Science, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, online textbook copies; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries on Akho's Chhappas and Gujarati literature; IGNOU, Eastern Philosophy, Block 1, section on Shuddhadvaita; Anishka Gheewala Lohiya, Pushtimarg in the UK and Gujarat, 2024; BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha, Scriptures of Our Sampradaya and general FAQs; Gujarat Tourism, Jalaram Temple Virpur; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Poetry, philosophical inquiry and service.

title: Gujarat's Saint-Poets and Devotional Traditions

body:
Religious interaction in Indian culture

Indian cultural history includes traditions originating within the subcontinent and traditions arriving from other regions through migration, trade and religious networks. These communities contributed to India's languages, architecture, education, commerce and social institutions.

The historical interaction of religious communities involved cooperation and mutual influence, but also disagreement and competition. Cultural exchange should not be understood as the complete disappearance of distinct religious identities.

Zoroastrianism and the Parsi community

Zoroastrianism is an ancient Iranian religious tradition associated with the prophet Zarathustra, also known as Zoroaster.

Its principal sacred literature is the Avesta. Zoroastrian teaching emphasises moral responsibility, truth and the ethical choice between good and evil. Ahura Mazda is the supreme divine being.

Its ethical ideals are commonly summarised through good thoughts, good words and good deeds.

Fire occupies a sacred position as a symbol associated with purity, truth and divine light. Zoroastrian religious practice maintains sacred fires in temples.

The religious significance of fire in Zoroastrianism should not be confused with the belief that physical fire itself is the supreme God.

Parsi settlement in Gujarat

Following major political and religious changes in Iran, groups of Zoroastrians migrated to the western coast of India. Their descendants became known as Parsis.

Sanjan in southern Gujarat occupies an important place in Parsi settlement traditions. The account of their migration and early settlement is preserved in the Persian narrative known as the Qissa-i-Sanjan.

The exact chronology of the earliest Parsi migration is not firmly established. Traditional accounts preserve important community memories but should not always be treated as exact contemporary historical records.

Udvada, in Valsad district, is a major Parsi religious centre. It houses the sacred Iranshah Atash Bahram, one of the most important fire temples of the Parsi community.

The Parsi community contributed to the commercial, industrial, educational and philanthropic history of Gujarat and western India.

Christianity in India

Christianity is centred on the teachings of Jesus Christ, with the Bible as its principal sacred scripture. Christian traditions emphasise faith, love, compassion and service, although their theological and institutional practices vary.

Christian communities established a historical presence in India through maritime connections and later through missionary activity. The Saint Thomas Christian tradition of Kerala traces its origins to the apostle Thomas, although the exact chronology of the earliest foundation is not independently established.

Christian institutions contributed to education, healthcare, printing and the development of regional-language literature, particularly during the modern period.

Regional and folk religious traditions of Gujarat

Gujarat's religious culture also includes local deities, sacred landscapes, village traditions and festivals. These often interact with wider Hindu religious traditions while retaining distinctive regional identities.

Goddess worship provides an important example. Ambaji in Banaskantha and Kalika Mata at Pavagadh in Panchmahal are major centres of Shakta devotion. Other forms of goddess worship are associated with local communities and regional traditions.

Garba expresses a connection between religious devotion and communal performance. Traditionally associated with Navaratri and goddess worship, it brings together devotional music, collective participation and symbolic reverence for divine feminine power.

Religion as a source of cultural expression

Different religious traditions have encouraged distinct forms of cultural production:

TraditionCultural expression
BuddhismStupas, monastic architecture and Jataka narratives
JainismTemple complexes, manuscript libraries and religious painting
Vaishnava BhaktiPads, Bhajans, Garbis and temple traditions
ShaktismGoddess shrines and Navaratri devotional traditions
SufismKhanqahs, Dargahs and devotional poetry
ZoroastrianismFire temples and Parsi religious institutions

These cultural expressions illustrate how philosophical and religious beliefs become visible in institutions, artistic forms and everyday community life.

Prelims focus

  • Zarathustra is associated with Zoroastrianism.
  • The Avesta is its principal sacred literature.
  • Sanjan is associated with early Parsi settlement traditions.
  • Udvada in Valsad district houses the Iranshah Atash Bahram.
  • Ambaji and Kalika Mata at Pavagadh are important goddess pilgrimage centres.
  • Trap: Udvada is a Parsi religious centre, not a Jain or Buddhist pilgrimage site.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, p. 73; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, sections on religious interaction; Gujarat Tourism, Udvada Parsi Fire Temple, 50 Golden Destinations of Gujarat and Religious Sites; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 7, Social Science, Chapter 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
